prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, taking atomic frequency standards to the 10^-18 level of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B024 as a single part, credited to Katori and Ye. After reading all eight round-1 statements the case looks stronger to me than before, because five members prefer it and none of the three who prefer other candidates argues that it is wrong or immature. Their objections concern what kind of discovery it is. On the science, the decisive step is Katori's magic-wavelength condition, which makes the light shift of the trapping field cancel for the clock transition and so allows many neutral atoms to be interrogated at once without the Doppler and recoil problems that limit free atoms. The first strontium lattice clock demonstration followed in 2005. The decisive step for the measurement is the improvement of roughly two orders of magnitude to the 10^-18 level, which required characterising blackbody radiation shifts, lattice-induced shifts and density shifts in a way other groups could repeat. That repetition has happened in Sr, Yb and Hg clocks in several countries, with clock-to-clock comparisons and fibre links, so the number is credible in the sense I care about as an experimentalist. The result also changes what can be measured, with gravitational redshift resolved over millimetre-to-centimetre height differences, tighter limits on drifting constants and on ultralight dark matter, and a many-body regime in the clock that has to be understood to improve it. I would write the citation around the invention and its realization, with the accuracy level as the demonstrated consequence, and without any reference to the redefinition of the second.
statement.case_against: The honest objections are unchanged but sharper after round 1. First, novelty: Danielsson, Eriksson and Mehlig see an extraordinary refinement of a capability that the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize already opened. I think that is a fair description of the lineage and an unfair description of the invention, but it is a judgment the committee has to make and not a fact. Second, the credit boundary: a two-name credit passes over Lemonde, Takamoto, Ovsiannikov, Ludlow, Hinkley and the ion-clock groups, and the line between Katori's concept and Ye's record accuracy is not razor-sharp, because much of the 10^-18 achievement is systematics control. Third, B003 has a case I take seriously: a new regime of matter was found after a specific prediction. If the committee believes that a discovery of a phenomenon should outrank a leap in a measurement capability, B003 is the natural next prize, and the open mechanism question is the main reason I would have it wait. Fourth, the redefinition of the second remains pending, although I do not think it is a condition.

responses.point: Eriksson asked whether the redefinition of the second is a necessary condition for the timing of a clock prize, and said he could support an instrument-driven prize this year.
responses.response: My answer is no, it is not necessary, and I would prefer that it not appear in the citation. The prize should be for what was demonstrated: a clock design whose systematic shifts can be controlled to the 10^-18 level, and independent clocks that agree at that level. The redefinition depends on the metrology institutions, on comparisons between remote clocks, and on the choice of species, and none of that changes the physics that was demonstrated. If the redefinition is delayed, the invention stands; if it happens, nobody is surprised. I also take his point about kind. I only ask that the committee not treat 'new phase of matter' as the sole route to a discovery. Making an observable that was out of reach measurable is also a discovery, and the clock comparisons already resolve effects of general relativity in a laboratory.

responses.point: Lindroth pressed me on whether the many-body and interaction physics of the clock, which Ye's group developed, belongs in the citation, and she would resist adding the SYRTE and NIST names.
responses.response: I considered it and now think the citation should not name many-body physics explicitly. The physics is real: s-wave and p-wave interactions, spin-orbit effects in the lattice and collective shifts stood between the early clocks and 10^-18. But it was a necessary route to the accuracy rather than the reason for the prize, and naming it invites the committee to ask for a separate scientific case and a larger credit list, which we cannot support with three names. I would keep it in the committee's background text, where it supports the argument that this is physics and not only engineering, and keep the citation short. On the credit boundary I agree with her: adding SYRTE or NIST names breaks the three-name limit and does not change who invented and realised the scheme.

responses.point: Olsson accepts the Katori and Ye division of labour but wants the citation worded around the invention and realization, not around accuracy records, and wants the first Sr demonstrations checked.
responses.response: I agree with the wording and have adjusted my citation: invention and realization come first, and the 10^-18 level follows as the demonstrated outcome. On the historical check, my reading is that the Sr lattice clock with the magic wavelength was first demonstrated by Katori's group in Tokyo, and that SYRTE and JILA reproduced and extended it within a short time. That is independent confirmation, not a competing invention. Lemonde's SYRTE group was early in the Sr and Hg lattice work, and Ovsiannikov contributed theory on magic wavelengths. I do not see anything in that record that moves the invention away from Katori, though I have not seen the primary priority documents here and the committee should check them. Ye's group is the clearest case where a later realization pushed the performance into a new regime, and for me that counts as realization in the citation's sense.

responses.point: Mehlig doubts the committee can separate Katori's concept from Ye's record accuracy and asks whether Ye's work is invention or systematics control, although he would not seriously oppose the clock prize.
responses.response: I think the separation is possible, and the answer is that both parts belong in the credit. Katori supplied the concept and the first realization. Ye's contribution was not only engineering: his group showed how a lattice clock behaves as a many-body system, used a three-dimensional lattice and later cavity-enhanced approaches to control the interaction shifts, and made stability and uncertainty near 10^-18 something other laboratories could match. Without that, the idea would still be a proposal at a much poorer accuracy. Where I concede ground is that a sceptic can describe the pair as bracketing one single advance. I think that is acceptable for a two-name prize, since the Nobel Prize has often rewarded an idea together with the group that made it work.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B003 for its new phenomenon, but says he would be content to see B024 first and would not resist it.
responses.response: I appreciate that, and I think B003 is a real candidate for a later year. My difficulty is the same as in round 1: the superconducting mechanism and the sample dependence of the phase diagram are still moving, and I would rather the committee write a citation about a settled discovery. If the committee wanted a two-part prize I would not object to B003 as a second part in principle, but the supplied credits would need five names in total, and I would not drop Bistritzer just to fit the three-name limit. So for 2026 I would keep B024 alone and revisit B003 in one to three years.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept the lattice clock as a discovery distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, or see it as the next step in the same lineage; this is a judgment and I cannot settle it with data.

Whether a two-name credit is accepted as complete when Lemonde, Takamoto, Ovsiannikov and the ion-clock groups have claims on particular milestones. I judge that the invention and realization sit with Katori and Ye, but I have not seen the primary priority record in this exchange.
How much of Ye's contribution counts as invention and how much as systematics control; the citation wording partly hides this.
Whether B003 should be preferred in a later year once the superconducting mechanism is better understood, and whether Bistritzer would then be part of the credit.
I have not seen any quantitative experimental test of the Toner-Tu exponents for B006 and cannot judge it from my own experience.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1 and still relevant. I spent a year of my doctoral work in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder; Hall shared the 2005 prize, and Jun Ye is a close colleague and former collaborator of Hall at JILA, so there is a lineage connection to one credited candidate. I have no direct collaboration with Katori or Ye. I work in atomic and optical physics at Lund, which may bias me toward precision atomic physics, and several colleagues have also flagged proximity to their own fields. I leave it to the chair and committee to weigh whether this requires recusal; the support count has not influenced my judgment.
